final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
DONE — Recommendation: **hybrid. Do the daily training yourself, but buy structured expert eyes. Specifically: enroll in HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 ($300, 6 wks, online, starts 8/19/26 6:15pm) and run the 4-week DIY plan alongside it.** Do NOT go full DIY, and do not spend $2,400+ as the opening move.

Reasoning:

WHY NOT PURE DIY:
- Two separate problems that need opposite handling. Leash pulling is a mechanical skill anyone can teach. Reactivity is emotional, and the fix is desensitisation/counter-conditioning — which requires reading threshold distance and body language correctly in real time. Shelters advise professional help partly because reactivity work is easy to get wrong and can be dangerous if mishandled.
- The critical fork you cannot easily self-diagnose: **frustration reactivity vs. fear reactivity, which need opposite responses.** Frustrated greeters strain toward the other dog with forward energy and want to say hi; fearful dogs are trying to create distance. Getting it wrong slows progress or makes it worse. Notably, for a frustrated greeter, whisking the dog away out of sight can actually *increase* the intensity of the display — the standard "increase distance" advice backfires. An experienced instructor sorts this out in one session; an owner can guess wrong for months.
- Risk of the wrong tool. Aversive/e-collar approaches are widely marketed locally and can teach the dog that the sight of another dog predicts pain.

WHY NOT FULL-PRICE PRIVATE TRAINING YET:
- Nothing here suggests a hard case. 14 months old is peak adolescence — this is the normal age for this exact pair of problems. There is no bite history mentioned. Barking and lunging without injury is squarely inside what a $300 group course is designed for.
- The daily reps are unavoidably the owner's job regardless of who is hired. Paying $1,500-$4,200 does not remove the homework; it only buys better coaching on it.
- Border collie mix: high intelligence, high need for mental work. A large share of adolescent herding-breed leash trouble is unmet mental stimulation, and enrichment is a cheap first lever to pull before spending four figures.

ESCALATE TO PAID 1:1 (Wag'N'Train $1,500 6-pack, or D For Dogz $2,400) IF, after 4 weeks, ANY of:
- The dog cannot eat/take treats at ANY distance from another dog (means threshold is farther than the street allows — needs a pro to set up controlled setups)
- Any air-snap, bite, or contact with a dog or person → skip straight to a CBCC-KA/behaviour consultant, and note this also disqualifies him from the HSSV class
- Redirected biting onto the leash, the handler's arms, or clothing during an outburst
- Zero measurable change in threshold distance over the 4 weeks
- The owner feels physically unsafe or unable to hold the dog

BUDGET SEQUENCE: $300 (Top Dogs 1) → optional $300 (Top Dogs 2, in-person, real dogs) → escalate to private only if the above triggers fire. Sub-$650 covers most cases of this profile. A $190 one-off Zoom eval with Stacy (CBCC-KA) is a good middle step if a fast expert read on fear-vs-frustration is wanted before the class starts.

subtasks.title: Find South Bay CA trainers who handle leash reactivity — shortlist 3 with real prices
subtasks.description:
DONE — 3 options found, all force-free, all with real published prices. Full comparison in the report on the parent task.

**OPTION A — HSSV "Top Dogs Level 1" (best value, act now)**
Humane Society Silicon Valley, 901 Ames Ave, Milpitas. dogtraining@hssv.org
- $300 general registration. Six weeks, ONE session/week, all online via Zoom. First session 90 min, then 5x 50 min.
- Explicitly "designed specifically for dogs struggling with leash or barrier reactivity." Positive reinforcement; covers threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, emergency exits, coping skills.
- Eligibility: dogs 8 months+ (dog is 14 mo = fine); no prior bite history on dogs or people; for dogs who "bark, lunge, or worry" but have not caused injury.
- **A cohort starts Wed 08/19/2026 at 6:15pm** — evening, fits the schedule. Register: https://pro.gofundme.com/event/e826622
- Follow-on: Top Dogs Level 2, $300, six weeks, 50 min/week, IN PERSON, small controlled group — this is where real-dog practice happens. Level 1 is the prerequisite.
- NOTE: HSSV's cheap $100 3-week "Loose Leash Walking & Reliable Recall" class is explicitly marked NOT appropriate for leash-reactive dogs. Do not book it.

**OPTION B — Stacy's Wag'N'Train (best credentials, 1:1)**
Stacy Braslau-Schneck, MA, CPDT-KA, **CBCC-KA**, CAP2. San Jose since 1998. wagntrain.com | Stacy@wagntrain.com
Listed on the SF SPCA's private-trainer referral list with leash-reactivity named as a specialty. CBCC-KA is the behavior-consultant credential — the right one for reactivity.
- Behavior Consultation/Evaluation, 1 hr Zoom: $190 alone, free inside any package
- "4-pack" $800 (4x 1hr) — basic training only, NOT behavior mod; likely insufficient
- "Beginning Behavior Modification 6-pack" **$1,500** (6x 1hr, eval + 5, 1-2 wks apart) — the realistic entry point
- "Behavior Modification Foundation" $3,000 (14x 1hr) — explicitly targets leash-reactivity + barking
- Follow-on sessions $130 each after a package ($145 standard). Virtual $145/hr.
- Serves San Jose, Willow Glen, Campbell, Santa Clara, Los Gatos, Los Altos, Saratoga, Cupertino, Mountain View, Milpitas. In-home books 2-3 weeks out.
- VERIFY BY EMAIL: site's "accepting new clients" banner was stale (June/July 2025). Confirm current availability + evening/weekend slots.

**OPTION C — D For Dogz (most intensive, most expensive)**
KT / Kaajal. Phone **650-538-3011**. dfordogtraining.com. Serves the whole South Bay incl. San Jose, Sunnyvale, Santa Clara, Campbell, Cupertino, Mountain View, Los Gatos.
- Dedicated "Leash Reactive Dog Foundations" private program:
  - **Private Coaching $2,400 / 6 weeks** — 90-min initial consult + weekly coaching sessions on real-world walks in YOUR neighborhood + between-session phone/text/email access. This is the you-do-the-training version.
  - Day Training $4,200 / 6 weeks — trainer works your dog 2x/week, you join every 3rd session, incl. a free group class + 3 months post-training support.
- **Free 15-minute discovery call** with KT — zero-cost way to sanity-check.
- Hours Mon-Fri 9am-7pm, Sun 9am-3pm (so weekday evening + Sunday coverage).

**RULED OUT — Off Leash K9 Training San Jose** (dogtrainerssanjose.com): $500 first lesson bundled with an e-collar, $100/session after. E-collar/aversive-based. Aversive tools on a dog that is barking out of arousal or fear risk making the dog associate pain with the sight of other dogs. Not recommended here.

subtasks.title: Build the week-by-week 4-week training plan
subtasks.description:
DONE — full 4-week plan written up in the report on the parent task; each week is also broken out as its own child subtask below.

CORE DESIGN LOGIC (read once, then follow the weekly subtasks):

1. **Split the walk in two.** The single biggest error is trying to train loose-leash walking and reactivity on the same outing. Reactivity work must happen below threshold; a normal walk is above threshold. So: "sniff walks" (dog's needs met, zero training expectations, quiet routes) + short separate "training reps." Never combine.

2. **Threshold is the whole game.** Threshold = the distance at which the dog can notice another dog but not "lose their brain." Over threshold, the dog physically cannot learn. For most leash-reactive dogs the starting threshold is roughly 50-100 ft. Practical field test: if he takes a treat, you're under threshold; if he won't eat, you are too close — leave, no exceptions.

3. **The protocol is Engage-Disengage / "Look At That" (LAT).** Two levels:
   - LEVEL 1: the instant he LOOKS at the other dog, mark ("yes!" or click) and feed. Deliver the treat so that taking it turns his head away from the trigger.
   - LEVEL 2: he looks at the dog; wait 3-5 seconds for him to look away ON HIS OWN; mark the disengagement and feed. If he doesn't look away within 5 seconds, drop back to Level 1.
   - Progression rule: 3-5 successful reps, then move 1-5 steps closer. Small increments only. If he reacts, you moved too fast — back up.
   The point: the sight of another dog starts predicting chicken instead of a fight.

4. **Diagnose fear vs. frustration in Week 1 — it changes the plan.** Frustrated greeter = strains forward, wants to get to the dog, body loose/wiggly, often fine once he arrives. Fearful = trying to create distance, weight back, hard stare, hackles. This matters because for a frustrated greeter, hustling him away out of sight can *escalate* the display rather than calm it — the usual "just increase distance" advice partially backfires. For frustration you lean harder on impulse control and teaching that calm gets access; for fear you lean harder on distance and never pushing.

5. **Mental work is not optional for this breed.** Adolescent border collie mix. Under-stimulated herding dogs escalate on leash. Sniffing and puzzle work tire this dog faster than distance walking, and food-based enrichment is a cheaper lever than more mileage.

6. **Absolute rule for all 4 weeks: no on-leash greetings.** Head-on leashed approaches are unnatural — dogs naturally greet in an arc, not face-on, and leash tension amplifies the whole thing. Many professionals run a blanket no-on-leash-greeting policy. Tell approaching owners "he's in training" and move on.

7. **Trigger budget.** Every blow-up sets you back days (stress hormones persist well beyond the moment). Aim for ZERO over-threshold reactions per week. A week with no outbursts beats a week with more training and three explosions.

subtasks.title: Gear check — get the 5 things before Week 1 starts
subtasks.description:
Buy/confirm before starting. Total roughly $60-100.

1. **Front-clip (no-pull) harness** — e.g. Balance Harness, Freedom, Easy Walk, Ruffwear Front Range. Front attachment redirects a pulling dog sideways instead of letting them lean into the pressure. This is MANAGEMENT, not a fix, but it makes weeks 1-2 physically survivable.
2. **Fixed-length 6ft leash** (nylon or biothane). NO retractable/flexi — you cannot control threshold distance with one.
3. **Optional: double-ended leash** to clip to both the front ring and the collar for extra steering control.
4. **High-value soft treats** — real chicken, cheese, hot dog, freeze-dried liver. NOT kibble, NOT dry biscuits. Must be pea-sized and swallowable in under a second so you can get a high rate of reinforcement. Buy more than feels reasonable.
5. **Treat pouch** that clips to your waist and stays open. Fumbling in a pocket loses the 1-second timing window that makes marker training work.

**DO NOT BUY:** prong collar, choke chain, or e-collar. On a dog that barks/lunges at other dogs, an aversive risks teaching him that the sight of another dog predicts pain, which can worsen reactivity or convert frustration into fear. (Side note: Stacy's Wag'N'Train runs PPG 'Project tRade' — you can trade in a prong/choke/shock collar for 10% off her services if you already own one.)

Optional: a clicker. A clear verbal marker ('YES!') works fine and is one less thing to hold.

subtasks.title: Week 1 — Decompress, diagnose the trigger, and stop rehearsing the blow-ups
subtasks.description:
GOAL: zero reactive outbursts this week. You are not training the reactivity yet, you are stopping the practice of it. Every rehearsal makes the habit stronger.

**Management (all week):**
- Walk at low-traffic times and routes — early morning, late evening, industrial streets, empty school lots. Weekends: drive somewhere quiet rather than walking the neighbourhood.
- Cross the street, turn around, or duck behind a parked car BEFORE he locks on. You are aiming to never get close enough for an outburst.
- No dog parks. No on-leash greetings. No pet store aisles.

**Daily (15-20 min total, split up):**
- 'Find it' game at home: toss a treat, say 'find it', repeat. This becomes your emergency escape hatch in Weeks 2-4 — you'll use it to move him past a dog with his nose down.
- Name response / auto check-in: say his name once in a quiet room, mark and feed the instant he turns. 10 reps. Then repeat in the yard, then on the quiet street.
- Hand-target ('touch'): present flat palm, mark+feed when his nose bumps it. This gives you a way to move his head and body away from a trigger without pulling.

**Enrichment (daily, non-negotiable for a border collie mix):**
- One 20-min 'sniffari' — a long-line decompression walk somewhere quiet where he sets the pace and sniffs whatever he wants. No training, no corrections.
- Feed at least one meal out of a snuffle mat, puzzle toy, or scattered in the grass instead of a bowl.

**DIAGNOSTIC — the main deliverable of Week 1.** Keep a note on your phone. For every dog sighting log: (a) distance in feet, (b) did he eat a treat, yes/no, (c) body language — straining FORWARD, loose/wiggly, whining, tail high and fast-wagging = FRUSTRATION; weight shifted BACK, hard stare, stiff, hackles up, trying to increase distance = FEAR. Also log time of day and whether the other dog was moving toward you.
By Sunday you should be able to state: 'his threshold is about ___ feet' and 'this is mostly frustration / mostly fear.' You need both numbers before Week 2 and the trainer will ask for them.

subtasks.title: Week 2 — Start Engage-Disengage at Level 1, well under threshold
subtasks.description:
GOAL: he sees a dog at distance, and his first instinct becomes looking back at you.

**Setup:** Pick a spot where dogs are predictable but far away — a bench at the far edge of a park, a parking lot overlooking a trail, the far corner of a field. Sit/stand at MORE than the threshold distance you measured in Week 1 (add 20% for safety). You want the dog to appear at distance, not round a corner at 10 feet.

**The rep (Engage-Disengage, LEVEL 1):**
1. Other dog comes into view.
2. The INSTANT he looks at it → mark ('YES!') → feed.
3. Deliver the treat so eating it turns his head away from the trigger (hold it low and slightly behind you).
4. Repeat every time he looks. High rate of reinforcement — you can't over-pay here.
5. If he won't eat: you are too close. Leave immediately and add distance next time. Not eating is the single clearest signal that he's over threshold.

**Dosage:** 3-4 sessions this week, 5-10 minutes each. Stop while he's still succeeding. These are SHORT. Do not do this on the same outing as his sniff walk.

**Progression rule:** 3-5 clean successful reps at a distance → move 1-5 steps closer. Not 20 feet closer. If he reacts, you went too fast — back up to where he was succeeding and bank more reps there.

**Also this week — loose-leash mechanics, separately, in the house/yard/quiet cul-de-sac only:**
- Leash-pressure release: apply the gentlest possible tension to the leash on the front-clip harness, and the moment he moves in a way that slackens it, mark and treat. Repeat. You're teaching that light pressure means 'come with me', not 'brace against this'. Eye contact not required.
- 'Be a tree': the instant the leash goes tight while walking, stop dead. Do not pull back. Wait. The moment there's slack, mark and walk on. Forward motion is the reward; pulling must never produce it.
- 5-10 min a day, boring environments only. Do not attempt loose-leash training on a street with dogs on it — you'll lose both skills at once.

**Continue all Week 1 management and enrichment.** The quiet routes stay quiet routes.

subtasks.title: Week 3 — Move to Engage-Disengage Level 2, add the emergency exit
subtasks.description:
GOAL: he chooses to look away from another dog by himself, and you have a reliable way to bail out of a bad situation.

**Engage-Disengage LEVEL 2 (upgrade from Week 2):**
1. He looks at the other dog.
2. Do NOT mark yet. Wait 3-5 seconds for him to look away on his own.
3. The moment he disengages by himself → mark → big treat.
4. If he doesn't look away within 5 seconds, he's too close or too aroused — drop back to Level 1 for the rest of that session.
5. Same progression rule: 3-5 clean reps, then close the distance by a few steps.

Level 2 is the real milestone — it's the difference between you managing his attention and him regulating himself.

**Emergency U-turn (practice on boring streets with NO dogs present, 10 reps a day):**
- Cheerful cue ('this way!' / 'let's go!') → pivot 180° → jog 5-10 steps → jackpot of 3-4 treats.
- Make it a fun game with zero triggers first. It must be automatic before you need it. This is your escape hatch when a dog appears around a corner inside threshold.
- Pair with the 'find it' game from Week 1: scatter treats on the ground to get his nose down and move him past a parked trigger.

**Reality check on 'surprise' triggers:** you will get ambushed by an off-leash dog or a corner. Use the U-turn, don't panic, and don't count it as failure — count it in your log.

**If you enrolled in HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 starting 8/19, you're mid-course by now.** Bring your Week 1 log (threshold distance, fear vs. frustration read) to the instructor and ask them directly whether your read is right. That single question is most of the value of the course.

**Loose leash — take it outside:** move the Week 2 exercises to real but quiet sidewalks. Add direction changes, turns and serpentines so he has to actually track where you're going. Still no busy dog-heavy routes.

**Continue:** sniffari, food puzzles, no on-leash greetings.

subtasks.title: Week 4 — Close distance deliberately, then measure progress and decide
subtasks.description:
GOAL: a measurably shorter threshold distance, and an evidence-based decision about whether to spend money on 1:1 training.

**Training:**
- Keep running Engage-Disengage Level 2, but now deliberately work the distance down in small increments. Target: comfortably passing a calm dog on the far side of a normal residential street.
- Add PARALLEL WALKING if you can borrow a friend with a calm, non-reactive dog: both dogs walk the same direction, wide apart, no face-to-face, gradually narrowing over several sessions. Never head-on — dogs naturally greet in an arc and head-on approaches are what escalate things.
- Start layering the two skills: on a quiet street with an occasional distant dog, ask for loose-leash walking, and switch to Engage-Disengage the moment a dog appears. This is the first week you combine them at all.
- Keep sessions short. Still no on-leash greetings — this stays a permanent policy, not a phase.

**MEASURE (do this on Saturday):**
Re-run the Week 1 diagnostic and compare directly:
- Threshold distance now vs. Week 1: ____ ft vs ____ ft
- Number of full outbursts in Week 4 vs Week 1: ____ vs ____
- Can he take a treat at the distance that made him explode in Week 1? Y/N
- Does he look at a distant dog and then look back at you unprompted? Y/N

**DECIDE:**
- **Clear improvement** (threshold shrinking, fewer outbursts, self-disengaging) → keep going solo; book HSSV Top Dogs Level 2 ($300, in-person, 6 wks) for supervised practice around real dogs. That's the natural next step.
- **Some progress but stalled / you're unsure of your own timing** → book Stacy Braslau-Schneck's $190 one-hour Zoom eval (CBCC-KA) or D For Dogz's FREE 15-min call (650-538-3011) for a read before committing to a package.
- **No change at all, OR any of the red flags** (won't eat at ANY distance; redirected biting onto leash/your arms/clothing; any snap or contact with a dog or person; you feel physically unsafe) → stop DIY and book private behaviour work: Wag'N'Train 6-pack $1,500 or D For Dogz Private Coaching $2,400/6wks. A bite history also disqualifies him from the HSSV group classes, so it changes the whole route.

Realistic expectation: 4 weeks buys a noticeably shorter threshold and fewer explosions. It does not buy a dog who is neutral about other dogs. Full reactivity rehab is months. Judge on trajectory, not arrival.
